claim: The crystal structure of the reconstituted yeast nucleosome shows a canonical structure that is largely indistinguishable from the first published one.
source: The crystal structure of the reconstituted yeast nucleosome (White et al., 2001) shows a canonical structure that is largely indistinguishable from the first published one (Luger et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to White et al., 2001 and Luger et al., 1997

claim: Canonical nucleosomes resemble 10-nm-wide, 6-nm-thick cylinders.
source: Canonical nucleosomes resemble 10-nm-wide, 6-nm-thick cylinders, and have 145–147 base pairs of DNA bent in 1.65 left-handed superhelical gyres around the histone octamer (Zhou et al., 2019; Zlatanova et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Zhou et al., 2019 and Zlatanova et al., 2009

claim: Canonical nucleosomes have 145–147 base pairs of DNA bent in 1.65 left-handed superhelical gyres around the histone octamer.
source: Canonical nucleosomes resemble 10-nm-wide, 6-nm-thick cylinders, and have 145–147 base pairs of DNA bent in 1.65 left-handed superhelical gyres around the histone octamer (Zhou et al., 2019; Zlatanova et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Zhou et al., 2019 and Zlatanova et al., 2009

claim: Non-canonical nucleosomes have either partially detached DNA, partially detached histones, fewer than eight histones, or a combination of these features.
source: In contrast, non-canonical nucleosomes have either partially detached DNA, partially detached histones, fewer than eight histones, or a combination of these features (Zlatanova et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zlatanova et al., 2009

claim: X-ray crystallography and single-particle cryo-EM have shown that reconstituted nucleosomes are largely canonical in vitro.
source: Both X-ray crystallography and single-particle cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) have shown that reconstituted nucleosomes, either alone or within a complex, are largely canonical in vitro (Zhou et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhou et al., 2019

claim: Nucleosome structures in situ inside cells remain mysterious.
source: Nucleosome structures in situ inside cells remain mysterious.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field

claim: Variation in linker DNA structure is a source of chromatin conformational heterogeneity.
source: Variation in linker DNA structure is a source of chromatin conformational heterogeneity (Collepardo-Guevara and Schlick, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Collepardo-Guevara and Schlick, 2014

claim: Recent cryo-EM studies show that nucleosomes can deviate from the canonical form in vitro, primarily in the structure of DNA near the entry/exit site.
source: Recent cryo-EM studies show that nucleosomes can deviate from the canonical form in vitro, primarily in the structure of DNA near the entry/exit site (Bilokapic et al., 2018; Fukushima et al., 2022; Sato et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bilokapic et al., 2018; Fukushima et al., 2022; Sato et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2021

claim: Nucleosomes in vitro have small changes in histone conformations.
source: In addition to DNA structural variability, nucleosomes in vitro have small changes in histone conformations (Bilokapic et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bilokapic et al., 2018

claim: Larger-scale variations of DNA and histone structure are not compatible with high-resolution analysis and may have been missed in single-particle cryo-EM studies.
source: Larger-scale variations of DNA and histone structure are not compatible with high-resolution analysis and may have been missed in single-particle cryo-EM studies.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential limitations of previous studies

claim: Cryo-electron tomography generates 3D reconstructions called cryotomograms at molecular-resolution (2–4 nm).
source: Molecular-resolution (2–4 nm) studies of unique objects like cells may be obtained by cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET), a form of cryo-EM that generates 3D reconstructions called cryotomograms.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cryo-ET capabilities

claim: Cryo-ET reveals life-like snapshots of macromolecular complexes because samples are prepared and imaged in an unfixed, unstained, frozen-hydrated state.
source: These studies reveal life-like snapshots of macromolecular complexes because the samples are prepared and then imaged in an unfixed, unstained, frozen-hydrated state.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cryo-ET methodology

claim: Most eukaryotic cells are too thick for cryo-ET, so thinner frozen-hydrated samples are made by cutting by cryomicrotomy or thinning by cryo-focused ion beam milling.
source: Most eukaryotic cells are too thick for cryo-ET, so thinner frozen-hydrated samples are made by cutting by cryomicrotomy or thinning by cryo-focused ion beam (cryo-FIB) milling (Ng and Gan, 2020; Strunk et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ng and Gan, 2020; Strunk et al., 2012

claim: Cryomicrotomy produces cryosections and cryo-FIB milling produces plank-like samples called cryolamellae.
source: These two approaches respectively produce cryosections and plank-like samples called cryolamellae.
evidence: This is established knowledge about sample preparation methods

claim: Large macromolecular complexes such as ribosomes and proteasomes have been identified in situ by 3D classification followed by comparison of the class averages to known structures.
source: Large macromolecular complexes such as ribosomes and proteasomes have been identified in situ by 3D classification followed by comparison of the class averages to known structures – an approach called purification in silico (Beck and Baumeister, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Beck and Baumeister, 2016

claim: Canonical nucleosomes exist in cryotomograms of yeast cell lysates ex vivo and in a HeLa cell cryolamella.
source: Using the purification in silico approach, we previously showed that canonical nucleosomes exist in cryotomograms of yeast cell lysates ex vivo and in a HeLa cell cryolamella (Cai et al., 2018a; Cai et al., 2018b; Cai et al., 2018c).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work by the authors (Cai et al., 2018a; Cai et al., 2018b; Cai et al., 2018c)

claim: 3D structural analysis did not generate canonical nucleosome structures from cryosectioned fission yeast cells.
source: However, our 3D structural analysis did not generate canonical nucleosome structures from cryosectioned fission yeast cells (Cai et al., 2018b).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work by the authors (Cai et al., 2018b)

claim: The authors hypothesized that yeast nucleosomes are either conformationally or constitutionally heterogeneous.
source: As a biological explanation for the absence of canonical nucleosome class averages in situ, we hypothesized that yeast nucleosomes are either conformationally or constitutionally heterogeneous.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors

claim: Budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae has only two copies of each histone gene.
source: We use the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, herein called yeast, because it has only two copies of each histone gene and because it is more amenable to gene editing.
evidence: This is established knowledge about yeast genetics

claim: Budding yeast is more amenable to gene editing than other organisms.
source: We use the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, herein called yeast, because it has only two copies of each histone gene and because it is more amenable to gene editing.
evidence: This is established knowledge about yeast as a model organism

claim: Canonical nucleosomes are abundant in nuclear lysates of the H2A-GFP-expressing strain and have extra densities consistent with GFP.
source: Canonical nucleosomes are abundant in nuclear lysates and, in the H2A-GFP-expressing strain's nuclear lysates, have extra densities consistent with GFP.
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by data shown in figures

claim: Canonical nucleosomes account for less than 10% of the expected number of total nucleosomes in wild-type cell cryolamellae.
source: In contrast, canonical nucleosomes account for less than 10% of the expected number of total nucleosomes in wild-type cell cryolamellae.
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by data and calculations

claim: Neither canonical nucleosomes nor nucleosome-like particles with extra protruding densities were detected in the H2A-GFP-expressing strain in situ.
source: Furthermore, neither canonical nucleosomes nor nucleosome-like particles with extra protruding densities were detected in the H2A-GFP-expressing strain.
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by data shown in figures

claim: The yeast intracellular environment disfavors the canonical nucleosome conformation.
source: These findings suggest that the yeast intracellular environment disfavors the canonical nucleosome conformation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings

claim: The subtomogram average of wild-type yeast nucleosomes in nuclear lysates has longer linker DNA than the crystal structure.
source: The subtomogram average of wild-type yeast nucleosomes in nuclear lysates has longer linker DNA (Figure 1B) than the crystal structure, which was reconstituted using a 146 bp DNA fragment.
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by data shown in Figure 1B

claim: The nucleosome-repeat length of budding yeast chromatin is ~168 bp.
source: Because the nucleosome-repeat length of budding yeast chromatin is ~168 bp (Brogaard et al., 2012), this extra length of DNA may come from an ordered portion of the ~22 bp linker between adjacent nucleosomes.
evidence: Supported by citation to Brogaard et al., 2012

claim: The extra length of DNA in the subtomogram average may come from an ordered portion of the ~22 bp linker between adjacent nucleosomes.
source: Because the nucleosome-repeat length of budding yeast chromatin is ~168 bp (Brogaard et al., 2012), this extra length of DNA may come from an ordered portion of the ~22 bp linker between adjacent nucleosomes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the nucleosome-repeat length

claim: Cryo-FIB milling is a compression-free method to thin frozen-hydrated cells.
source: Cryo-FIB milling is a compression-free method to thin frozen-hydrated cells (Hayles et al., 2007; Mahamid et al., 2015; Marko et al., 2006; Medeiros et al., 2018; Rigort et al., 2010; Villa et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hayles et al., 2007; Mahamid et al., 2015; Marko et al., 2006; Medeiros et al., 2018; Rigort et al., 2010; Villa et al., 2013

claim: Cryo-FIB milling uses a beam of gallium ions to thin a cell under cryogenic conditions, producing a frozen-hydrated plank-like cellular sample called a cryolamella.
source: This technique uses a beam of gallium ions to thin a cell under cryogenic conditions, producing a frozen-hydrated plank-like cellular sample called a cryolamella.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cryo-FIB milling methodology

claim: Canonical nucleosomes are detectable in a HeLa cell cryolamella.
source: Canonical nucleosomes are detectable in a HeLa cell cryolamella (Cai et al., 2018a), meaning that cryo-FIB milling does not grossly perturb canonical nucleosomes in situ.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work by the authors (Cai et al., 2018a)

claim: Cryo-FIB milling does not grossly perturb canonical nucleosomes in situ.
source: Canonical nucleosomes are detectable in a HeLa cell cryolamella (Cai et al., 2018a), meaning that cryo-FIB milling does not grossly perturb canonical nucleosomes in situ.
evidence: This is an inference based on the detection of canonical nucleosomes in HeLa cell cryolamellae

claim: Two-dimensional class averages of template-matched nucleosome-like particles from wild-type yeast cryolamellae reveal densities that have the approximate size and shape of nucleosomes.
source: Two-dimensional class averages of template-matched nucleosome-like particles reveal densities that have the approximate size and shape of nucleosomes (Figure 1—figure supplement 5, panel A).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5, panel A

claim: None of the 3D class averages from wild-type yeast cryolamellae resemble canonical nucleosomes when using the original RELION classification workflow.
source: However, none of these 3D class averages resemble canonical nucleosomes (Figure 1—figure supplement 5, panel B).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5, panel B

claim: Direct 3D classification using 100 classes did not reveal any canonical nucleosome class averages in wild-type yeast cryolamellae.
source: To rule out the possibility that canonical nucleosomes were missed during 2D classification, we performed direct 3D classification using 100 classes. None of the resultant 100 class averages resemble a canonical nucleosome (Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6

claim: Template matching and classification using the yeast nucleosome crystal structure as a reference did not reveal canonical nucleosome class averages in wild-type yeast cryolamellae.
source: No canonical nucleosome class averages were seen in this control experiment (Figure 1—figure supplement 7, panels B and C).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 7, panels B and C

claim: VPP data has more low-resolution contrast than defocus phase-contrast data.
source: VPP data has more low-resolution contrast than defocus phase-contrast data.
evidence: This is established knowledge about VPP imaging

claim: Subtomogram analysis of VPP tomograms by 2D classification followed by 3D classification did not reveal a canonical nucleosome class average in wild-type yeast cryolamellae.
source: Subtomogram analysis of the VPP tomograms by 2D classification (Figure 1—figure supplement 9, panel A), followed by 3D classification did not reveal a canonical nucleosome class average in BY4741 (Figure 1—figure supplement 9, panel B).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 9

claim: Direct 3D classification using 100 classes on VPP data detected one class average that resembles a canonical nucleosome in wild-type yeast cryolamellae.
source: When we performed direct 3D classification using 100 classes, we detected one class average that resembles a canonical nucleosome (Figure 1—figure supplement 10, panel A, Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 10, panel A

claim: A second round of classification revealed two types of class averages, one of which resembles a slightly elongated nucleosome.
source: A second round of classification revealed two types of class averages, one of which resembles a slightly elongated nucleosome (Figure 1—figure supplement 10, panel B, Figure 1—video 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 10, panel B

claim: Refinement of the two types of nucleosomes produced 24 Å resolution averages that differ in the amount of linker DNA visible.
source: Refinement of these two types of nucleosomes produced 24 Å resolution averages that differ in the amount of linker DNA visible (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 10, panel C).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 10, panel C

claim: The class average that has more ordered linker DNA vaguely resembles the chromatosome.
source: The class average that has more ordered linker DNA vaguely resembles the chromatosome, a form of the nucleosome that has linker DNA crossing at the entry-exit site and in contact with a linker histone (Bednar et al., 2017; Zhou et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an observation from the study, with citations to Bednar et al., 2017; Zhou et al., 2015 for the definition of chromatosome

claim: The DNA does not appear to cross at the DNA entry-exit site in the class average with more ordered linker DNA.
source: However, the DNA does not appear to cross at the DNA entry-exit site, and, at the present resolution, it is not possible to determine if the linker histone is present.
evidence: This is an observation from the study

claim: At the present resolution, it is not possible to determine if the linker histone is present in the class average with more ordered linker DNA.
source: However, the DNA does not appear to cross at the DNA entry-exit site, and, at the present resolution, it is not possible to determine if the linker histone is present.
evidence: This is a limitation of the study

claim: Complexes in situ are not subject to orientation biases from the air-water interface.
source: Unlike plunge-frozen complexes, which interact with the air-water interface and have biased orientations (Noble et al., 2018), complexes in situ are not subject to such biases.
evidence: Supported by citation to Noble et al., 2018

claim: The disc views of canonical nucleosomes are undersampled and likely missed by the classification analysis.
source: Visualization of the angular distribution of the canonical nucleosomes shows that the disc views are undersampled and likely missed by the classification analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 10, panel D), which we also observed in our analysis of HeLa nucleosomes in situ (Cai et al., 2018a).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 10, panel D and citation to Cai et al., 2018a

claim: The missing hemisphere of views results in roughly half of the canonical nucleosomes going undetected.
source: This missing hemisphere of views results in roughly half of the canonical nucleosomes going undetected.
evidence: This is an inference based on the angular distribution analysis

claim: The use of VPP and relatively thin cryolamellae made it possible to detect two canonical nucleosome classes that differ in the amount of ordered linker DNA.
source: In summary, the use of VPP and relatively thin (≤160 nm) cryolamellae made it possible to detect two canonical nucleosome classes that differ in the amount of ordered linker DNA, similar to what we observed in a HeLa cell (Cai et al., 2018a).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study, with citation to Cai et al., 2018a

claim: Template matching using the same reference as for nuclei analysis and then direct 3D classification into 100 classes did not reveal canonical nucleosome class averages in the cytoplasm.
source: We performed template matching using the same reference as for our analysis of nuclei and then direct 3D classification into 100 classes. None of the resultant class averages resemble a canonical nucleosome (Figure 1—figure supplement 12), confirming that our analysis was not biased by the cylindrical reference.
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 12

claim: The classification detected only 769 canonical nucleosomes in wild-type yeast cryolamellae.
source: Our classification detected only 769 canonical nucleosomes.
evidence: This is a finding from the study

claim: Accounting for the undersampling of disc views, there are an estimated ~1500 canonical nucleosomes detected in the five tomograms.
source: If we account for the undersampling of disc views (Figure 1—figure supplement 10, panel D), we estimate there are ~1500 canonical nucleosomes detected in the five tomograms.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the data

claim: In the single HeLa cell cryolamella cryotomogram, there were more than 2000 nucleosomes in a nucleus volume ~1/6th of the total analyzed in BY4741.
source: In comparison, we estimate that in the single HeLa cell cryolamella cryotomogram (Cai et al., 2018a), there were more than 2000 nucleosomes in a nucleus volume ~1/6th of the total analyzed here in BY4741.
evidence: This is a comparison with previous work, with citation to Cai et al., 2018a

claim: The canonical nucleosomes are scattered throughout the sampled nuclear volume in wild-type yeast cryolamellae.
source: The remapped model shows that the canonical nucleosomes are scattered throughout the sampled nuclear volume.
evidence: This is a finding from the study, based on remapping the class averages

claim: There are no large clusters of canonical nucleosomes like what was seen near the nuclear envelope of a HeLa cell.
source: There are no large clusters of canonical nucleosomes like what we saw near the nuclear envelope of a HeLa cell.
evidence: This is a comparison with previous work

claim: The tomograms analyzed are expected to hold 25,000 nucleosomes based on experimentally determined values for nucleosome number and chromatin volume.
source: Using experimentally determined values for nucleosome number and chromatin volume (Oberbeckmann et al., 2019; Uchida et al., 2011), the tomograms we analyzed are expected to hold 25,000 nucleosomes.
evidence: This is a calculation based on citations to Oberbeckmann et al., 2019; Uchida et al., 2011

claim: The nucleosomes should pack with an order-of-magnitude higher density than visualized in the remapped model.
source: Therefore, the nucleosomes (both canonical and non-canonical) should pack with an order-of-magnitude higher density than visualized in our remapped model (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the expected number of nucleosomes

claim: The vast majority (>90%) of the nucleosomes in BY4741 yeast are non-canonical.
source: In summary, our calculations suggest that the vast majority (>90%) of the nucleosomes in BY4741 yeast are non-canonical.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study, based on calculations

claim: Subtomogram 3D classification is sensitive to features much smaller than the nucleosomes, as evidenced by the separation of canonical nucleosome class averages that differ by ~10 bp of linker DNA near the dyad.
source: Our previous cryo-ET analysis of nucleosomes in a HeLa cell revealed that subtomogram 3D classification is sensitive to features much smaller than the nucleosomes, as evidenced by the separation of canonical nucleosome class averages that differ by ~10 bp of linker DNA near the dyad (Cai et al., 2018a).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work by the authors (Cai et al., 2018a)

claim: Studies of flagella and pilus machines showed that subtomogram averages of complexes in situ can reveal either the presence or absence of protein densities as small as fluorescent proteins.
source: Furthermore, studies of flagella (Oda and Kikkawa, 2013) and pilus machines (Chang et al., 2016) showed that subtomogram averages of complexes in situ can reveal either the presence or absence of protein densities as small as fluorescent proteins.
evidence: Supported by citations to Oda and Kikkawa, 2013 and Chang et al., 2016

claim: The tagging strategy did not work as intended because tagged nucleosome 3D classes could not be detected in situ.
source: Note that this tagging strategy did not work as intended because we could not detect tagged nucleosome 3D classes in situ.
evidence: This is a finding from the study

claim: An N-terminal GFP tag is not expected to be visible in subtomogram averages because it would be separated from the histone's globular domain by the long, flexible N-terminal 'tail'.
source: An N-terminal GFP tag is not expected to be visible in subtomogram averages because it would be separated from the histone's globular domain by the long, flexible N-terminal 'tail'.
evidence: This is an inference based on knowledge of histone structure

claim: GFP was fused to the histone C-terminus, which does not have a flexible tail.
source: Therefore, we fused GFP to the histone C-terminus, which does not have a flexible tail (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, panels A and B) and we further confined the GFP by eliminating the peptide linker that is included in popular GFP-tagging modules (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, panel C).
evidence: This is a methodological choice made by the authors, supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: S. cerevisiae has two copies of each histone gene.
source: S. cerevisiae has two copies of each histone gene (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, panel D), which are arranged as gene pairs.
evidence: This is established knowledge about yeast genetics, supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 1, panel D

claim: The H2A and H2B genes are arranged as gene pairs HTA1-HTB1 and HTA2-HTB2.
source: The H2A and H2B genes are arranged as gene pairs HTA1-HTB1 and HTA2-HTB2 (Hereford et al., 1979).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hereford et al., 1979

claim: The entire HTA2-HTB2 gene pair was deleted to prevent its amplification as circular DNA molecules by the flanking retrotransposon elements.
source: We deleted the entire HTA2-HTB2 gene pair to prevent its amplification as circular DNA molecules by the flanking retrotransposon elements (Libuda and Winston, 2006); the resulting strain is called LGY0012.
evidence: This is a methodological choice made by the authors, with citation to Libuda and Winston, 2006

claim: The GFP gene was inserted at the 3' end of HTA1, without a linker, to generate LGY0016, making H2A-GFP the sole source of H2A.
source: Next, we inserted the GFP gene at the 3' end of HTA1, without a linker, to generate LGY0016, making H2A-GFP the sole source of H2A.
evidence: This is a methodological step in the study

claim: LGY0016's genotype was confirmed by PCR analysis, Sanger sequencing, and immunoblots using anti-H2A or anti-GFP antibodies.
source: We confirmed LGY0016's genotype by PCR analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 2, panels A and B), Sanger sequencing, and immunoblots using anti-H2A or anti-GFP antibodies (Figure 3—figure supplement 2, panel C).
evidence: This is a methodological step in the study, supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: LGY0016 nuclei showed bright fluorescence.
source: Accordingly, the LGY0016 nuclei showed bright fluorescence (Figure 3—figure supplement 2, panel D).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 2, panel D

claim: The strain LGY0015 was constructed, which expresses both a H2B-GFP fusion without a linker peptide and an untagged copy of H2B.
source: We also constructed the strain LGY0015, which expresses both a H2B-GFP fusion without a linker peptide (Figure 3—figure supplement 2, panels E–H) and an untagged copy of H2B.
evidence: This is a methodological step in the study, supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: Strains that have either H2B-GFP, H3-GFP, or H4-GFP as the sole H2B, H3, and H4 sources, respectively, could not be created.
source: We were unable to create strains that have either H2B-GFP, H3-GFP, or H4-GFP as the sole H2B, H3, and H4 sources, respectively (see H3- and H4-tagging experiments below).
evidence: This is a finding from the study

claim: The LGY0016 doubling time is ~50% longer than for wild-type BY4741 (130 min versus 85 min) in rich media.
source: Consistent with this low tolerance for a GFP-tagged histone as the sole source of a histone type, the LGY0016 doubling time is ~50% longer than for wild-type BY4741 (130 min versus 85 min) in rich media.
evidence: This is a finding from the study

claim: The 2D class averages of LGY0016 and LGY0015 nuclear lysates resemble those seen in single-particle cryo-EM studies of reconstituted nucleosomes, though with lower-resolution features.
source: The 2D class averages of LGY0016 and LGY0015 nuclear lysates resemble those seen in single-particle cryo-EM studies of reconstituted nucleosomes (Chua et al., 2016), though with lower-resolution features (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 5, panel A).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, with citation to Chua et al., 2016, supported by Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 5, panel A

claim: Canonical nucleosome 3D class averages were obtained in the lysates of both LGY0016 and LGY0015 strains using direct 3D classification into 40 classes.
source: To increase the number of detected nucleosomes, we used direct 3D classification into 40 classes. We obtained canonical nucleosome 3D class averages this way in the lysates of both strains (Figure 3—figure supplements 6 and 7; Figure 1—videos 1 and 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by Figure 3—figure supplements 6 and 7

claim: The canonical nucleosome class averages from LGY0016 and LGY0015 lysates have the unmistakable structural motifs of canonical nucleosomes, such as a 10-nm-diameter, 6-nm-thick cylindrical shape, and the left-handed path of the DNA densities.
source: These class averages have the unmistakable structural motifs of canonical nucleosomes, such as a 10-nm-diameter, 6-nm-thick cylindrical shape, and the left-handed path of the DNA densities.
evidence: This is a finding from the study

claim: The canonical nucleosome class averages from LGY0016 and LGY0015 lysates have more DNA than the crystal structure's 1.65 gyres because lysate chromatin samples have linker DNA.
source: There is more DNA than the crystal structure's 1.65 gyres because lysate chromatin samples have linker DNA.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of extra DNA density

claim: Subsequent classification rounds revealed nucleosome class averages that have an extra density projecting from one or both faces in LGY0016 and LGY0015 lysates.
source: Subsequent classification rounds revealed nucleosome class averages that have an extra density projecting from one or both faces (Figure 3—figure supplement 6, panel B, and Figure 3—figure supplement 7, panel B).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 6, panel B, and Figure 3—figure supplement 7, panel B

claim: One example of each class (zero, one, or two extra densities) was refined to ~25 Å resolution in LGY0016 lysates.
source: One example of each class (zero, one, or two extra densities) was refined to ~25 Å resolution (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 5, panel B).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 5, panel B

claim: The position of the extra density is consistent with the H2A C-terminus being closer to the DNA entry-exit point.
source: The position of the extra density is consistent with the H2A C-terminus being closer to the DNA entry-exit point (Figure 3C) and the H2B C-terminus being far from the DNA entry-exit point (Figure 3—figure supplement 5, panel C).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 5, panel C

claim: The absence of LGY0015 nucleosome classes with two densities suggests that they are either unstable or too rare to detect by 3D classification.
source: In principle, LGY0015 cells can assemble nucleosomes that have two copies of H2B-GFP. The absence of LGY0015 nucleosome classes with two densities suggest that they are either unstable or too rare to detect by 3D classification.
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of certain classes

claim: The authors focused their in situ cryo-ET analysis on LGY0016 cells because the GFP tags are easier to recognize on nucleosomes from nuclear lysates of this strain.
source: We focused our in situ cryo-ET analysis on LGY0016 cells because the GFP tags are easier to recognize on nucleosomes from nuclear lysates of this strain.
evidence: This is a methodological choice made by the authors

claim: The 3D class averages from all three LGY0016 in situ samples resembled neither canonical nucleosomes nor cylindrical bodies with one or more protruding densities.
source: The 3D class averages from all three samples resembled neither canonical nucleosomes nor cylindrical bodies with one or more protruding densities that is expected from the lysate samples (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplements 4 and 5, Figure 4—video 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplements 4 and 5

claim: Some class averages from LGY0016 in situ samples have two linear motifs that resemble the double DNA gyres opposite the DNA entry-exit point, but these DNA-like densities do not go 1.65 times around the center of mass as expected of canonical nucleosomes.
source: Some class averages have two linear motifs that resemble the double DNA gyres opposite the DNA entry-exit point, but these DNA-like densities do not go 1.65 times around the center of mass as expected of canonical nucleosomes (Luger et al., 1997).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, with citation to Luger et al., 1997

claim: Small variations in the classification parameters such as mask size and class number did not reveal any canonical nucleosome classes in LGY0016 cell cryotomograms.
source: Small variations in the classification parameters such as mask size, class number did not reveal any canonical nucleosome classes in LGY0016 cell cryotomograms.
evidence: This is a finding from the study

claim: Canonical nucleosomes are rare inside budding yeast nuclei.
source: We therefore conclude that canonical nucleosomes are rare inside budding yeast nuclei and that non-canonical nucleosomes are the vast majority.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study

claim: Non-canonical nucleosomes are the vast majority inside budding yeast nuclei.
source: We therefore conclude that canonical nucleosomes are rare inside budding yeast nuclei and that non-canonical nucleosomes are the vast majority.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study

claim: The structures of the non-canonical nucleosomes are not known.
source: At present, we do not know what the non-canonical nucleosome structures are, meaning that we cannot even determine if one non-canonical structure is the majority.
evidence: This is a limitation of the study

claim: Subtomogram averaging of cytoplasmic ribosomes obtained a subtomogram average at ~33 Å resolution based on the FSC=0.5 cutoff criterion (or 28 Å using the FSC = 0.143 criterion), from 1150 particles.
source: Using our control tomogram of the cytoplasm, which is densely packed with ribosomes, we obtained a subtomogram average at ~33 Å resolution based on the Fourier shell correlation (FSC)=0.5 cutoff criterion (or 28 Å using the FSC = 0.143 criterion), from 1150 particles (Figure 4—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 6

claim: The ribosome subtomogram average has density features consistent with 15 Å to 30 Å resolution range.
source: As a comparison, we simulated densities with the yeast ribosome crystal structure between 15 Å and 30 Å resolution and found that our average has density features consistent with this resolution range.
evidence: This is a finding from the study

claim: The resolutions of the nucleosome and ribosome averages (~24 Å and 33 Å) are comparable to recent in situ subtomogram averages using similar numbers of particles (~500–1500).
source: The resolutions of our nucleosome and ribosome averages (~24 Å and 33 Å) are comparable to recent in situ subtomogram averages using similar numbers of particles (~500–1500) (Laughlin et al., 2022; van den Hoek et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Laughlin et al., 2022; van den Hoek et al., 2022

claim: The cryolamellae, data, and workflow do not show evidence of pathologies.
source: Therefore, our cryolamellae, data, and workflow do not show evidence of pathologies.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the ribosome control experiment

claim: The absence of nucleosome-like class averages that have an extra density bump in LGY0016 cryolamellae suggested that previously unappreciated properties of the H2A-H2B heterodimer make this histone pair a poor candidate for the GFP fusion tag strategy.
source: In cryolamellae of LGY0016 cells, the absence of nucleosome-like class averages that have an extra density bump suggested that previously unappreciated properties of the H2A-H2B heterodimer make this histone pair a poor candidate for the GFP fusion tag strategy (see Discussion).
evidence: This is an inference from the study

claim: All attempts to make H3- or H4-GFP 'sole source' strains failed.
source: Because all attempts to make H3- or H4-GFP 'sole source' strains failed, we tested strains that had one wild-type copy and one GFP-tagged copy of one of these histones.
evidence: This is a finding from the study

claim: The genotypes and phenotypes of H3-GFP and H4-GFP strains were verified by confirmation PCRs, western blots, Sanger sequencing, and fluorescence confocal microscopy.
source: The genotypes and phenotypes were verified by confirmation PCRs, western blots, Sanger sequencing (not shown), and fluorescence confocal microscopy (Figure 4—figure supplements 7 and 8).
evidence: This is a methodological step in the study, supported by Figure 4—figure supplements 7 and 8

claim: H3-GFP strains were created without a linker (LGY0007) and with linker sequences RIPGLIN (LGY0002) and GGSGGS (LGY0070).
source: We created H3-GFP strains without a linker (LGY0007) and with linker sequences RIPGLIN (LGY0002) and GGSGGS (LGY0070); this latter linker was introduced previously (Verzijlbergen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a methodological step in the study, with citation to Verzijlbergen et al., 2010

claim: A H4-GFP-expressing strain could only be obtained by using the flexible GGSGGS linker (LGY0071).
source: For H4, we could only obtain a strain with a H4-GFP-expressing strain by using the flexible GGSGGS linker (LGY0071; Figure 4—figure supplement 8).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 8

claim: Flexible linkers are not expected to facilitate tag-based identification because the tag can occupy a much larger volume and get blurred out.
source: Flexible linkers are not expected to facilitate tag-based identification because the tag can occupy a much larger volume and get blurred out as a result but was the only one tolerated in our H4 tagging attempts.
evidence: This is an inference based on knowledge of protein structure

claim: The lysates of each of the four H3-GFP and H4-GFP strains had large numbers of canonical nucleosomes.
source: Like the other strains, the lysates of each of these four strains had large numbers of canonical nucleosomes (Figure 4—figure supplements 9–12, panel A of each).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by Figure 4—figure supplements 9–12

claim: Class averages that have the extra density were only detected in the LGY0007 nuclear lysates.
source: Of the canonical nucleosomes, we were only able to detect class averages that have the extra density in the LGY0007 nuclear lysates (Figure 4—figure supplement 9); the nuclear lysates of the other strains do not have nucleosome class averages with a GFP density.
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 9

claim: The 3D class averages in LGY0007 cell cryolamellae resemble neither canonical nucleosomes nor cylindrical bodies with a protruding density.
source: Compared to the BY4741 (wild-type) cell cryolamella VPP class averages (Figure 1—figure supplement 10, panel A), the 3D class averages in LGY0007 cell cryolamellae resemble neither canonical nucleosomes nor cylindrical bodies with a protruding density (Figure 4—figure supplement 14).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 14

claim: H3- and H4-GFP fusions cannot be used to detect non-canonical nucleosomes.
source: Therefore, H3- and H4-GFP fusions cannot be used to detect non-canonical nucleosomes and much more work needs to be done to identify non-canonical nucleosomes.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study

claim: The earliest in situ studies of chromatin were done with projection cryo-EM images and 2D Fourier analysis of cryosectioned cells, which revealed that long-range order is absent in chromatin in situ.
source: The earliest in situ studies were done with projection cryo-EM images and 2D Fourier analysis of cryosectioned cells, which revealed that long-range order is absent in chromatin in situ (Eltsov et al., 2008; McDowall et al., 1986).
evidence: Supported by citations to Eltsov et al., 2008; McDowall et al., 1986

claim: Cryo-ET studies showed that short-range order is present in isolated chicken erythrocyte nuclei.
source: Cryo-ET studies later showed that short-range order is present in isolated chicken erythrocyte nuclei (Scheffer et al., 2011), but absent in picoplankton and budding yeast (Chen et al., 2016; Gan et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Scheffer et al., 2011

claim: Short-range order is absent in picoplankton and budding yeast.
source: Cryo-ET studies later showed that short-range order is present in isolated chicken erythrocyte nuclei (Scheffer et al., 2011), but absent in picoplankton and budding yeast (Chen et al., 2016; Gan et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chen et al., 2016; Gan et al., 2013

claim: Early cryo-ET studies revealed little about nucleosome structure in situ because the nucleosomes in those samples appeared like smooth ellipsoids.
source: These early cryo-ET studies revealed little about nucleosome structure in situ because, as Eltsov et al. observed, the nucleosomes in those samples appeared like smooth ellipsoids (Eltsov et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Eltsov et al., 2018

claim: Recent cryo-ET studies using state-of-the-art electron-counting cameras and energy filters have revealed that in cryotomographic slices of cell nuclei, there are densities that resemble nucleosome side and gyre views in which gyre-like features are resolved.
source: Recent cryo-ET studies using state-of-the-art electron-counting cameras and energy filters have revealed that in cryotomographic slices of cell nuclei, there are densities that resemble nucleosome side and gyre views in which gyre-like features are resolved (Cai et al., 2018a; Cai et al., 2018b; Eltsov et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cai et al., 2018a; Cai et al., 2018b; Eltsov et al., 2018

claim: Higher-fidelity data made it possible to use 3D classification to detect canonical nucleosomes in nuclear envelope-associated chromatin in a HeLa cell.
source: This higher-fidelity data made it possible to use 3D classification to detect canonical nucleosomes in nuclear envelope-associated chromatin in a HeLa cell (Cai et al., 2018a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cai et al., 2018a

claim: The use of 3D classification detected canonical nucleosomes in wild-type yeast nuclear lysates and canonical nucleosomes both with and without GFP tags in nuclear lysates of some strains that bear histone-GFP fusions.
source: Our use of 3D classification detected canonical nucleosomes in wild-type yeast nuclear lysates and canonical nucleosomes both with and without GFP tags in nuclear lysates of some strains that bear histone-GFP fusions.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the study

claim: A canonical nucleosome class average was detected in wild-type cell cryolamellae imaged with a VPP.
source: We also detected a canonical nucleosome class average in wild-type cell cryolamellae imaged with a VPP.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the study

claim: The in situ detections suggest that there are only ~1500 canonical nucleosomes out of the 25,000 nucleosomes expected of the total sampled nuclear volume.
source: The in situ detections suggest that there are only ~1500 canonical nucleosomes (taking account of the undersampling of nucleosomes in the disc view) out of the 25,000 nucleosomes expected of the total sampled nuclear volume.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the data

claim: The percentage of canonical nucleosomes in lysates cannot be accurately estimated because the total number of nucleosomes in each field of view cannot be determined.
source: Note that the percentage of canonical nucleosomes in lysates cannot be accurately estimated because we cannot determine how many nucleosomes in total are in each field of view.
evidence: This is a limitation of the study

claim: The estimates from the cryolamellae are more reliable because the expected numbers of nucleosomes can be estimated from genomics, biochemical, and X-ray tomography data.
source: The estimates from the cryolamellae are more reliable because the expected numbers of nucleosomes (canonical or not) can be estimated from genomics, biochemical, and X-ray tomography data (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is an explanation of the methodology

claim: Canonical nucleosome classes or any cylindrical nucleosome-sized structures that have extra density bumps were not detected in LGY0016 cell cryolamellae.
source: When we analyzed LGY0016 cell cryolamellae, in which H2A-GFP is the sole source of H2A, we did not detect canonical nucleosome classes or any cylindrical nucleosome-sized structures that have extra density bumps.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the study

claim: Analysis of cryolamellae of LGY0007 did not reveal either a canonical nucleosome-like class average or any cylindrical nucleosome-sized density with an extra density bump.
source: Likewise, analysis of cryolamellae of LGY0007 did not reveal either a canonical nucleosome-like class average or any cylindrical nucleosome-sized density with an extra density bump, even though H3-GFP should be incorporated into the H3-H4 tetramer, the central component of the nucleosome.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the study

claim: The absence of either a canonical nucleosome-like class average that has an extra density bump, or a cylinder with an extra density bump in the LGY0016 strain suggests that the H2A-H2B heterodimer is mobile in situ.
source: The absence of either a canonical nucleosome-like class average that has an extra density bump, or a cylinder with an extra density bump in the LGY0016 strain suggests that the H2A-H2B heterodimer is mobile in situ.
evidence: This is an inference from the study

claim: By 'mobility', the authors mean that H2A-H2B is attached to the rest of the nucleosome and can have small differences in orientation.
source: By 'mobility', we are not implying that H2A-H2B is dissociated. We mean that H2A-H2B is attached to the rest of the nucleosome and can have small differences in orientation.
evidence: This is a clarification of terminology

claim: Approximately 80% of H2B is bound to chromatin in situ.
source: The H2A/H2B heterodimers are in contact with the H3/H4 heterotetramer because crosslinking and single-particle fluorescence imaging experiments showed that approximately 80% of H2B – and presumably H2A to which it stably dimerizes – is bound to chromatin in situ (Mohan et al., 2018; Ranjan et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mohan et al., 2018; Ranjan et al., 2020

claim: H2A-H2B mobility was hinted at by the observations from X-ray crystallography that yeast nucleosomes lack the hydrogen bonds that stabilize the two H2A-H2B heterodimers in metazoan nucleosomes.
source: H2A-H2B mobility was hinted at by the observations from X-ray crystallography that yeast nucleosomes lack the hydrogen bonds that stabilize the two H2A-H2B heterodimers in metazoan nucleosomes (White et al., 2001) and that interfaces between H2A-H2B and H3 are moderately exposed to small-molecule probes (Marr et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to White et al., 2001 and Marr et al., 2021

claim: Interfaces between H2A-H2B and H3 are moderately exposed to small-molecule probes.
source: H2A-H2B mobility was hinted at by the observations from X-ray crystallography that yeast nucleosomes lack the hydrogen bonds that stabilize the two H2A-H2B heterodimers in metazoan nucleosomes (White et al., 2001) and that interfaces between H2A-H2B and H3 are moderately exposed to small-molecule probes (Marr et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Marr et al., 2021

claim: Recent simulations show that the H2A/H2B heterodimer may adopt numerous orientations and small displacements, with either fully or partially unwrapped DNA, while remaining in contact with H3-H4.
source: Furthermore, recent simulations show that the H2A/H2B heterodimer may adopt numerous orientations and small displacements, with either fully or partially unwrapped DNA, while remaining in contact with H3-H4 (Ishida and Kono, 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ishida and Kono, 2022

claim: The authors cannot rule out the possibility that expression of H2A-GFP makes nucleosomes less ordered in situ.
source: We also cannot rule out the possibility that expression of H2A-GFP makes nucleosomes less ordered in situ.
evidence: This is a speculation about a potential confounding factor

claim: None of the LGY0007 in situ nucleosome-like class averages had an extra density consistent with the GFP density tag.
source: Like LGY0016 (H2A-GFP sole source), none of the LGY0007 (H3 plus H3-GFP) in situ nucleosome-like class averages had an extra density consistent with the GFP density tag (only seen in lysates).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the study

claim: There were no canonical nucleosome class averages seen among the class averages of LGY0007 cell cryolamella nucleosome-like particles.
source: Furthermore, there were no canonical nucleosome class averages – either with or without the GFP density – seen among the class averages of LGY0007 cell cryolamella nucleosome-like particles.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the study

claim: The expression of H3-GFP makes nucleosomes less ordered in situ.
source: These observations suggest that the expression of H3-GFP makes nucleosomes less ordered in situ.
evidence: This is an inference from the study

claim: In budding yeast, canonical nucleosomes are rare in situ and the expression of GFP-tagged histones leads to further perturbations of nucleosome structure in situ.
source: Altogether, our experiments show that in budding yeast, canonical nucleosomes are rare in situ and that the expression of GFP-tagged histones leads to further perturbations of nucleosome structure in situ.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study

claim: The data is consistent with a model in which yeast canonical nucleosomes are abundant ex vivo.
source: Our data is consistent with a model in which yeast canonical nucleosomes are abundant ex vivo (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study, supported by Figure 5A

claim: Yeast nucleosomes adopt multiple non-canonical conformations in situ.
source: They adopt multiple non-canonical conformations in situ (Figure 5B and C) and rarely adopt the canonical one (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study, supported by Figure 5B, C, and D

claim: A high abundance of non-canonical nucleosomes means that more of the genome would be accessible, consistent with yeast having high levels of transcription.
source: A high abundance of non-canonical nucleosomes means that more of the genome would be accessible, consistent with yeast having high levels of transcription.
evidence: This is an inference based on the findings

claim: Nucleosome heterogeneity is consistent with the absence of chromatin long-range order in situ because crystalline oligonucleosome arrays can only form if sequential nucleosomes adopt nearly identical conformations.
source: Nucleosome heterogeneity is also consistent with the absence of chromatin long-range order in situ because crystalline oligonucleosome arrays can only form if sequential nucleosomes adopt nearly identical conformations (Ekundayo et al., 2017; Robinson et al., 2006; Song et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on the findings, with citations to Ekundayo et al., 2017; Robinson et al., 2006; Song et al., 2014

claim: Further investigation is needed to identify the biochemical and biophysical factors responsible for the abundance of non-canonical nucleosomes in yeast and to determine their diverse structures.
source: Further investigation is needed to identify the biochemical and biophysical factors responsible for the abundance of non-canonical nucleosomes in yeast and to determine their diverse structures (Zlatanova et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions, with citation to Zlatanova et al., 2009

claim: Globular complexes as small as canonical nucleosomes (~200 kDa) can be detected by 3D classification of subtomograms from cryolamellae that were imaged with a VPP.
source: In combination with our previous work on a HeLa cell (Cai et al., 2018a), we show that globular complexes as small as canonical nucleosomes (~200 kDa) can be detected by 3D classification of subtomograms from cryolamellae that were imaged with a VPP.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study, with citation to Cai et al., 2018a

claim: It is not yet feasible to systematically determine the conditions needed to detect sub-200 kDa complexes by purification in silico given the low throughput of cryo-FIB milling, the low yield of cryolamellae thinner than 160 nm, and the technical difficulties of VPP imaging.
source: Given the low throughput of cryo-FIB milling, the low yield of cryolamellae thinner than 160 nm, and the technical difficulties of VPP imaging, it is not yet feasible to systematically determine the conditions needed to detect sub-200 kDa complexes by purification in silico.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of current technology

claim: More depositions of eukaryote cryolamellae cryo-ET datasets in the public database EMPIAR may enable a thorough search of data collection and processing parameter space.
source: More depositions of eukaryote cryolamellae cryo-ET datasets in the public database EMPIAR (Iudin et al., 2016) may enable a thorough search of data collection and processing parameter space.
evidence: This is a speculation about future research, with citation to Iudin et al., 2016

claim: ChIP-seq analysis has detected sub-nucleosomes in situ, though the abundance was unknown.
source: ChIP-seq analysis has detected sub-nucleosomes in situ, though the abundance was unknown (Rhee et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rhee et al., 2014

claim: MNase-seq has detected nucleosomes in a partially unwrapped and partially disassembled state in situ.
source: MNase-seq has also detected nucleosomes in a partially unwrapped and partially disassembled state in situ (Ramachandran et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ramachandran et al., 2017

claim: A recent Hi-C variant 'Hi-CO' presented evidence that <147 bp of yeast nucleosomal DNA is protected from MNase attack.
source: A recent Hi-C variant 'Hi-CO' presented evidence that <147 bp of yeast nucleosomal DNA is protected from MNase attack (Ohno et al., 2019), which is consistent with the partial detachment of core DNA.
evidence: Supported by citation to Ohno et al., 2019

claim: Molecular dynamics advances in all-atom and coarse-grained simulations are now showing that nucleosomes are far more dynamic than previously appreciated.
source: Molecular dynamics advances in all-atom and coarse-grained simulations are now showing that nucleosomes are far more dynamic than previously appreciated (Armeev et al., 2021; Brandani et al., 2021; Farr et al., 2021; Huertas et al., 2021; Ishida and Kono, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Armeev et al., 2021; Brandani et al., 2021; Farr et al., 2021; Huertas et al., 2021; Ishida and Kono, 2021

claim: The DNA-unwrapping associated with nucleosome breathing was shown to disfavor ordered helical oligonucleosome structures.
source: The DNA-unwrapping associated with nucleosome breathing was shown to disfavor ordered helical oligonucleosome structures (Farr et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Farr et al., 2021

claim: Nucleosome breathing is evident in high-throughput atomic force microscopy experiments, which revealed that only ~30% of nucleosomes are fully wrapped, and that approximately half of the nucleosomes have an opening angle 60° larger than the fully wrapped one.
source: Nucleosome breathing is also evident in high-throughput atomic force microscopy experiments, which revealed that only ~30% of nucleosomes are fully wrapped, and that approximately half of the nucleosomes have an opening angle (measured between the entry/exit DNA arms) 60° larger than the fully wrapped one (Konrad et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Konrad et al., 2021

claim: Nucleosomes that have non-canonical nucleosome properties, such as lower stability or exposure of internal surfaces, have been reported in fission yeast.
source: Nucleosomes that have non-canonical nucleosome properties, such as lower stability or exposure of internal surfaces, have been reported in fission yeast (Koyama et al., 2017; Sanulli et al., 2019), which may explain why we did not observe canonical nucleosomes in cryosections in those cells either (Cai et al., 2018b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Koyama et al., 2017; Sanulli et al., 2019; Cai et al., 2018b

claim: Some nucleosomes in human and fly cell cryosections appear 'gaping', that is, with the inter-DNA-gyre distance slightly larger than ~2.7 nm.
source: Some nucleosomes in human and fly cell cryosections appear 'gaping', that is, with the inter-DNA-gyre distance slightly larger than ~2.7 nm (Eltsov et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Eltsov et al., 2018

claim: Partial DNA detachment has been seen in complexes between nucleosomes and remodelers and transcription factors.
source: Partial DNA detachment has been seen in complexes between nucleosomes and remodelers and transcription factors (Eustermann et al., 2018; Farnung et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2017; Sundaramoorthy et al., 2018; Sundaramoorthy et al., 2017; Willhoft et al., 2018), methyltransferases (Bilokapic and Halic, 2019; Jang et al., 2019), or transcription-related complexes (Dodonova et al., 2020; Kujirai et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Eustermann et al., 2018; Farnung et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2017; Sundaramoorthy et al., 2018; Sundaramoorthy et al., 2017; Willhoft et al., 2018; Bilokapic and Halic, 2019; Jang et al., 2019; Dodonova et al., 2020; Kujirai et al., 2018

claim: Larger amounts (up to ~25 bp) of DNA detachment have been seen very rarely in cryo-EM structures.
source: Larger amounts (up to ~25 bp) of DNA detachment have been seen very rarely in cryo-EM structures (Bilokapic et al., 2018; Zhou et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bilokapic et al., 2018; Zhou et al., 2021

claim: A recent study of cryosectioned fly embryos has presented evidence of nucleosome-like structures such as hemisomes and three-gyre structures.
source: A recent study of cryosectioned fly embryos has also presented evidence of nucleosome-like structures such as hemisomes and three-gyre structures (Fatmaoui et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fatmaoui et al., 2022

claim: The prevalence and functional consequences of non-canonical nucleosomes in situ remain to be studied in other organisms.
source: The prevalence and functional consequences of non-canonical nucleosomes in situ remain to be studied in other organisms.
